sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Interactive Lab 1! Scroll down directly below this slide to experiment with our real-time latency decomposition and bottleneck throughput profiler.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Lab 1, Kaito! Tune the micro-batch window and dynamic GPU batch size to see how batching unlocks forty-fold higher throughput while keeping end-to-end latency strictly under the 200-millisecond SLA!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Interactive Lab 2! Scroll down directly below this slide to explore HDFS NameNode heap footprint, test quorum split-brain safety, and track Out-of-Vocabulary token drift.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Lab 2, Kaito! See how compacting small files slashes NameNode heap from 30 gigabytes down to 1.5 megabytes, test read and write quorum overlap, and raise stream OOV to trigger the 3-sigma tokenizer retraining alert!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 1! A streaming pipeline records 15 milliseconds ingest, 100 milliseconds buffer, 25 milliseconds GPU inference, and 30 milliseconds commit. What is total end-to-end latency, and what is the optimal micro-batch interval with 50-millisecond dispatch overhead at 5,000 events per second? Select Option A, Option B, or Option C.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 1, Kaito! Add up the four latency stages to check SLA compliance, and compute the square root formula for optimal micro-batching. Look at the options below!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Outstanding systems derivation! Summing 15, 100, 25, and 30 milliseconds gives exactly 170.0 milliseconds, comfortably within the 200-millisecond SLA! And taking the square root of 2 times 0.050 divided by 5,000 times 0.002 yields exactly 100.0 milliseconds for optimal micro-batch scheduling!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Double-check your latency summation and square root formula! Total latency is 15 plus 100 plus 25 plus 30, which equals 170.0 milliseconds. For optimal micro-batching, 2 times 0.050 is 0.10, divided by 10.0 is 0.01, and the square root of 0.01 is 0.100 seconds, or 100 milliseconds.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 2! In an end-to-end pipeline, Kafka delivers 20,000 events per second, disk sinks sustain 76,800 events per second, and 4 GPU workers run unbatched inference at 20 milliseconds per pass. Identify current throughput, and calculate the minimum batch size needed at 30 milliseconds per pass to match Kafka. Select Option A, Option B, or Option C.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 2, Kaito! Four GPUs divided by 0.020 seconds sustains only 200 events per second. How large must dynamic GPU batch size B scale to saturate Kafka's 20,000 events per second?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Spot-on throughput analysis! In unbatched mode, 4 GPUs at 20 milliseconds sustain only 200 events per second, creating a severe bottleneck! To match Kafka's 20,000 events per second at 30 milliseconds per pass, we solve 4 times B divided by 0.030 greater than or equal to 20,000, which yields a minimum batch size of exactly 150 items per forward pass!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Review Definition 9.10.2! Unbatched GPU capacity is 4 divided by 0.020, which is 200 events per second. To reach 20,000 events per second, 4 times B divided by 0.030 must equal 20,000. Multiplying 20,000 by 0.030 gives 600, and dividing by 4 gives a required batch size of 150 items.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 3! A topic replicates across 5 brokers with write quorum 3. What is the minimum read quorum required to prevent split-brain reads? And if rolling token monitoring detects an Out-of-Vocabulary rate of 6.20% against a 1.30% Upper Control Limit, what is the anomaly z-score? Select Option A, Option B, or Option C.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 3! For 5 replicas and 3 writes, R plus W must strictly exceed 5. And for OOV drift, calculate the z-score of 6.20% relative to standard error 0.000995. Select your answer below!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Flawless distributed systems and statistical reasoning! For N=5 and W=3, R plus 3 strictly greater than 5 requires minimum read quorum R=3, ensuring at least one overlapping replica! Furthermore, an OOV rate of 6.20% against baseline 1.0% divided by standard error 0.000995 produces a massive positive 52.26 sigma anomaly, triggering automated tokenizer retraining!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Check your quorum inequality and z-score calculation! By the pigeonhole principle, R plus W must strictly exceed N, so R plus 3 greater than 5 means R must be at least 3. For drift, 0.0620 minus 0.0100 is 0.0520, and dividing by standard error 0.000995 yields positive 52.26 sigma.
